prize_parts.citation: for the optical lattice clock: magic-wavelength trapping of neutral atoms and its development to a fractional uncertainty of 10^-18, verified between independent laboratories

statement.case_for: After the full first-round exchange I keep the same configuration: B029 alone, Katori and Ye. Four of us reached it independently, and the four who prefer other candidates still name it as a serious alternative, which tells me the scientific case survives scrutiny from different directions. I am not counting heads, though; what matters is the physics. Katori's insight is that at a particular wavelength the trapping light shifts the two clock levels equally, so the lattice does not disturb the transition. That is a statement from atomic structure theory, and it turns thousands of atoms into one oscillator without Doppler or recoil broadening. Ye's group then showed that this many-atom system can be controlled to about 10^-18, including the regime where interactions between the atoms matter. The test I trust most is that clocks in different laboratories, built differently, agree when compared, and that has been done between JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, NIST and SYRTE. In round 1 the chair asked whether the proposal history changes the two names. As someone who has worked on the theory of these levels, I do not think it does: Lemonde and Peik contributed to the early discussion of lattice clocks, but the magic-wavelength scheme as a concrete, testable route to a low-uncertainty clock is Katori's, and the demonstration at the limit is Ye's. On wording, I now accept Kroll's point in part: the citation should name both the concept and its realisation at 10^-18, but should stay tied to the neutral-atom lattice so that it does not claim comb or ion-clock work. As to waiting for the redefinition of the second, I would not make it a condition. The recognition rests on what has already been demonstrated, and a clock that is compared across continents is already a result, whatever metrology bodies decide later.
statement.case_against: The objection I cannot dismiss is the one Olsson, Eriksson and Mehlig press: that the 2005 and 2012 prizes already paid for the comb and for single-ion control, so a lattice clock is a continuation. I think the answer is that the lattice clock uses a different mechanism (the magic wavelength and many-atom statistics), but this is a judgement about degree, and a reasonable colleague can weigh it the other way. Eriksson's wording, that this is a refinement of precision spectroscopy more than a new behaviour of matter, is fair as a description of the field, and I should not overstate the unexpectedness. This is not a discovery of the kind where nature surprises us, as high-harmonic generation did. Attribution also has a tail that a two-name credit cannot remove: Ludlow, Bloom, Lemke, Hinkley and the ion-clock groups did essential work, and the best ion clocks still compete on accuracy. Finally, I have to repeat that this is my own subfield. I am therefore more cautious with my own enthusiasm than with the cases I cannot judge, and I note that the strongest sceptics on novelty are colleagues from outside atomic physics, whom I should take seriously.

responses.point: Pearce asked me directly whether the proposal history (Lemonde, Peik and others) is adequately represented by crediting only Katori and Ye, and said he would be comfortable if Kroll and I think so.
responses.response: I do think so, with one qualification that I want recorded. The earlier discussions of optical lattice clocks (Lemonde and Peik among them) described the idea of a lattice clock but did not provide the wavelength condition that makes the trapped transition free of the trap's own light shift in a way that can be tested; Katori's 2001-2003 scheme did, and he followed it with an experiment. On the other side, the 10^-18 result is a team effort at JILA, and Nobel practice is to credit the group leader who defined the programme. The two-name set does not claim that others did nothing. I would not ask for an outside assessment to change the names, but if the Secretary commissions one, the question to put to the assessors is the priority of the magic-wavelength condition, and I expect it to confirm Katori.

responses.point: Olsson ranks the clock last and argues that novelty is limited by the 2005 and 2012 prizes and that the benefit to humanity is currently modest, while her own preference is the NV centre.
responses.response: I have tried to take the novelty argument at its strongest. It is true that the comb made optical frequencies countable and that Wineland showed control of single ions. The lattice clock needed neither new counting nor single-particle control: it needed the realisation that a many-atom trap can be made free of its own perturbation, and that is why the stability gain is so large. As to benefit, I accept that clocks have not yet changed daily life and that NV sensing has more visible applications now. I would not let that decide it, though: the Physics Prize is for the discovery, and when it is made nobody knows the uses. I also noted in round 1 that NV centres have a stronger practical record, and I still agree. My remaining doubt about B001 is the boundary of the discovery (single-spin detection versus the later sensing field) and the position of Lukin and others, which you have described yourself as unsettled, whereas the clock's credit set is narrower.

responses.point: Eriksson treats B029 as a serious alternative with the strongest reproducibility and the cleanest credit, but regards it as a refinement of precision spectroscopy rather than a new behaviour of matter, and prefers B031.
responses.response: I agree with the first half and partly with the second. Where I disagree is on 'refinement': when a measurement moves by two orders of magnitude it opens up new physical questions, such as the gravitational redshift over a millimetre and the many-body interactions of the atoms inside the clock, which were not accessible before. I accept that flat-band superconductivity is a more surprising result about matter, and that it has been reproduced widely. My difficulty with B031 is not that the physics is wrong but that I lack the expertise to judge the maturity of the interpretation, and both you and Mehlig say the mechanism is open and that Cao, Dean and others are outside the set. I still list B031 as my first alternative. If you and Mehlig can say how many independent groups have seen superconductivity at the magic angle, that would affect my view of it more than anything I could say about clocks.

responses.point: Danielsson proposes B029 together with a single-laureate B037 (Halzen, IceCube) as two distinct achievements within three names, and presses me on B016 where I ranked topological insulators second while deferring to condensed-matter colleagues.
responses.response: On B016, you are right and I withdraw some of my second-place weight: the credit set (Kane, Mele, Molenkamp, Hasan, with the late Zhang and the HgTe prediction by Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang) is exactly the kind of dispute I cannot resolve from atomic physics, and I keep B016 as an alternative only. On your configuration, I welcome B029 as a part, but I cannot give an independent judgement on B037: the credit to one name for a large observatory is a question for you and Pearce, and the unknown origin of most of the flux makes me hesitant. I see no scientific kinship between a clock and a neutrino telescope, and I would not choose the second part just to use the third name. I would rather the committee have one prize the whole committee can defend than two parts where one has a single doubtful credit.

responses.point: Kroll agrees on the two names and proposes that the citation should be written around the measurement achievement (control of systematics to 10^-18) and not around the idea alone.
responses.response: I accept this and have changed my citation: it now names the magic-wavelength trapping and its development to 10^-18, verified between laboratories. My concern was that a citation for the achievement could appear to cover the whole of optical clocks, so I have kept the neutral-atom lattice in the wording. On the question the chair put to both of us, whether the ion-clock credit alters the two-name set, my answer is no, because the ion clocks are a different route. We agree that the citation should not suggest that ion clocks were derived from the lattice or the reverse.

responses.point: Johansson asked me to separate the question of scientific merit from the question of sequence for circuit QED, which I ranked sixth because of the 2025 prize, and described the clock as a metrological refinement.
responses.response: That is a fair challenge to my own reasoning. I accept that sequence is not a scientific argument, and I will say plainly that circuit QED is a real, new regime and that its theory and first experiments were well before the 2025 work. My remaining concerns are only practical: the four-to-three credit problem, which you solve by dropping Girvin but that the record does not settle for me, and your own closeness to the field, which you have flagged and which I assume you will handle with the chair. So my view is that B004 is a serious candidate whose weaknesses are of credit and not of science, and I do not regard the 2025 prize as decisive. I still do not agree that the clock is only a refinement, for the reasons I gave to Eriksson, but I have not moved to B004 because I cannot settle the third name.

responses.point: Mehlig prefers B031 on the strength of a transparent analytic prediction followed by a decisive experiment, but names B029 as the cleaner two-name fallback if the credit set for B031 is judged unsound.
responses.response: I appreciate the fairness of naming B029 as the fallback, and I think the structure of your argument is right: a quantitative prediction that was then confirmed is the strongest kind of discovery. My concern is the one you list yourself, which is that three names cannot cover Bistritzer-MacDonald, the early commensurate-angle theory, and the experimental groups of Cao, Fatemi and Dean. If the committee prefers a two-name pair, MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero, I would regard that as a cleaner credit than the trio, but then Bistritzer's contribution to the prediction would not be recognised, which seems to me a harder explanation. For me this is the deciding comparison between the two: I am comfortable that B029 can be defended in public on its record today, whereas B031 depends on a credit judgement I cannot make.

uncertainties: Whether the committee sees the lattice clock as new enough given the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize, which is a judgement of degree on which colleagues differ
Whether Katori and Ye are the right pair, or whether the team contributions (Ludlow, Bloom, Lemke, Hinkley) and the proposal-history contributions (Lemonde, Peik) should change the credit
How the committee weighs a measurement advance, whose payoff via a redefinition of the second is still pending, against a discovery of new quantum behaviour such as flat-band superconductivity
Whether B031 is mature enough and how many independent groups have reproduced magic-angle superconductivity, on which I defer to Eriksson and Mehlig
Whether a second prize part would add anything scientifically, since I do not see a kinship between B029 and B037 and cannot judge B037 myself
statement.conflict_note: Unchanged from round 1. I am a long-time close collaborator of Anne L'Huillier (2023 laureate) and have co-authored with the Lund attosecond group and with Ursula Keller's group at ETH. None of these is a credited name in B029, B031 or B016, so I see no recusal issue for my preferred configuration. My work on atomic many-body theory and on theory for storage-ring and attosecond experiments is adjacent to B029, B044 and B018, and the committee should weigh my preference for B029 with that in mind. I have no connection to Katori, Ye or their groups that I would regard as a conflict, and none to the credited names of B031 or B016.
